Keno Basics: Odds, Payouts, and Why the House Edge Runs So High

Published September 15, 2026 · 8 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Keno looks like the friendliest game on the floor. Pick some numbers, wait for a drawing, see how many you matched — no strategy chart, no dealer interaction to navigate, no minimum bet that stings. That simplicity is exactly why it's worth understanding the math before you play more than a few dollars of it, because keno's house edge sits in a completely different neighborhood than almost anything else a casino offers. Here's how the game is actually built, how its pay tables work, and why the number that decides your long-run odds is so much worse than blackjack's or even roulette's.

How a keno game actually works

Standard keno uses an 80-number field. Players choose a set of numbers — usually referred to as "spots" — typically somewhere between one and ten, though some pay tables allow up to fifteen or twenty. A drawing then selects 20 numbers out of the 80, either by a certified random number generator online or, in a live keno lounge, by an actual ball-draw machine. Your payout depends on how many of your chosen numbers, or "spots," appear among the 20 drawn — a match is usually called a "catch."

Online and video keno draw rapidly and repeatedly, often every minute or faster, which is a very different pace than the lottery-style keno drawings some casinos and state lottery systems run every few minutes on a shared schedule. The underlying math is identical either way; only the speed at which you're exposed to it changes.

How payouts scale with your "catches"

Every keno variant runs on a published pay table tied to how many spots you picked. A ticket where you picked 10 spots and catch all 10 typically pays a huge multiple of your wager — sometimes thousands of times the bet — but catching four or fewer numbers on that same 10-spot ticket usually pays nothing at all. A smaller ticket, say a 4-spot pick, pays modestly for catching two, three, or all four, with nothing like the outsized jackpot potential of a bigger spot count.

That structure is deliberately back-loaded toward rare, high-catch outcomes, in the same spirit as a lottery ticket: most of a keno pay table's advertised excitement lives in outcomes you'll rarely hit, while the bulk of actual rounds pay nothing or return a small fraction of the original bet.

Reality check: keno's pay tables are built to make the big multiplier feel reachable, but the odds of catching enough numbers to hit it are considerably longer than most players intuitively assume from picking "just" 8 or 10 numbers out of 80.

Why keno's house edge runs so high

Combine a low probability of hitting the higher-catch outcomes with a pay table that doesn't fully compensate players for how rare those outcomes actually are, and you get a house edge that's dramatically wider than almost any other casino game. Depending on the specific pay table and how many spots you pick, keno's house edge commonly runs somewhere in the 20% to 35%-plus range. That's not a typo relative to other casino math — it's an order of magnitude worse than a well-played table game.

The comparison matters because keno doesn't look like a 20%-plus-edge game while you're playing it. It feels closer to a lottery scratcher or a bingo card, low-key and inexpensive per ticket, which tends to obscure just how steep the long-run math actually is.

Comparing keno's edge to other casino games

GameTypical house edge
Blackjack (basic strategy)~0.5%

Baccarat (banker bet)~1.06%
Roulette (single-zero)~2.7%
Roulette (double-zero)~5.26%
Keno (typical pay tables)~20%–35%+

For more on how those other figures are calculated, see our guides on house edge across casino games and craps basics. Keno's position on that list is a good reminder that "low minimum bet" and "low house edge" are two completely unrelated things.

Straight tickets vs. way tickets

A straight ticket is the simplest version: you pick one set of numbers and bet on that combination outright. Live keno lounges in some casinos also offer "way tickets" or combination tickets, which group your chosen numbers into multiple overlapping sub-bets on a single ticket — for example, splitting twelve numbers into several smaller groups, each acting as its own separate wager with its own separate payout. Way tickets let you cover more small-win combinations at once, at the cost of spreading your total stake across more, generally smaller, individual bets. They're mostly a live-keno-lounge feature; most online keno games stick to straight, single-ticket bets.

Common mistakes and misconceptions

The most common mistake is assuming a 10-spot ticket's high-catch odds scale in some intuitive, roughly-linear way from a 4-spot ticket's odds — they don't, and the gap widens fast as you add spots. A second is underestimating keno's edge because the game feels similar to bingo or a lottery scratcher, both of which most players already correctly assume are long-shot, low-payback formats; keno deserves that same mental framing, not the "just a fun side game" treatment it sometimes gets. A third is chasing the marquee big-multiplier payout by consistently maxing out spot counts without appreciating how rarely that outcome actually lands. And a fourth is thinking that a live keno lounge's periodic drawing schedule, versus an online game's much faster RNG-driven pace, changes the underlying odds — it doesn't. Pace changes how quickly you're exposed to the house edge, not the edge itself, the same gambler's-fallacy-adjacent mistake covered in more detail in our casino game myths guide.

Frequently asked questions

Is there a "best" number of spots to pick in keno?

Not meaningfully. The house edge stays high across most standard pay tables regardless of how many spots you choose, though the exact figure shifts slightly by spot count and by casino.

Is online keno mathematically different from live casino or lottery keno?

No. The underlying odds and house edge come from the same combinatorics either way; online keno's random number generator is independently tested and certified much like a slot machine's, it just draws far more frequently.

Do other players' number choices affect my payout?

No. Casino keno pays out against a fixed pay table, not a shared prize pool split among players, so what numbers other people pick has no effect on what you win.

Does picking numbers that haven't been drawn recently improve my odds?

No. Every keno drawing is an independent random event with no memory of past draws, so a number's recent history has no bearing on whether it's more or less likely to be drawn next.

Why do casinos even offer a game with such a high house edge?

It draws players looking for a low-cost shot at a large multiplier, similar to a lottery ticket, and it requires far less floor space and staffing than a live table game, which makes it worth offering even at a small betting minimum.
